\section{\label{sec:level1}Introduction}
Heat conduction in materials has traditionally been described by Fourier’s law, which postulates that the heat flux, $\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)$, arises instantaneously and linearly in response to local temperature gradients, $\vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}, t)$. This assumption leads to the diffusive evolution of temperature fields in both space and time, governed by the following set of foundational equations~\cite{fourier1888theorie,carslaw1959conduction}:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:classic_theory}
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:conservation}
\rho c \, \frac{\partial T(\vec{r},t)}{\partial t} + \vec{\nabla}_{r} \cdot  \vec{j} (\vec{r}, t) = 0, \\
\label{eq:Fourier_law}
\vec{j}(\vec{r},t) = - \overleftrightarrow{\kappa}_\text{bulk}(\vec{r}) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r}, t),\\
\label{eq:Green-Kubo}
\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}_\text{bulk} = \frac{V}{k_B T_0^2} \langle \vec{j}_\text{bulk}(t) \otimes \vec{j}_\text{bulk}(0) \rangle_\text{eq},
\end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}
where $\rho$ is the mass density and $c$ is the specific heat capacity per unit mass. Equation~\eqref{eq:Green-Kubo}, known as the Green–Kubo relation~\cite{green1954markoff,dong2001_PhysRevLett.86.2361}, expresses the bulk thermal conductivity tensor $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}_\text{bulk}$ in terms of the time-autocorrelation of the fluctuating bulk heat flux $\vec{j}_\text{bulk}$, averaged over an equilibrium ensemble at temperature $T_0$. The prefactor involves the Boltzmann constant $k_{\text{B}}$ and the system volume $V$, which together normalize the microscopic fluctuations to yield a macroscopic transport coefficient.

%However, these approaches assume local response and neglect the intrinsically nonlocal and history-dependent nature of thermal transport across material inhomogeneities.

Real materials often exhibit spatial variations in structure, composition, and transport properties. Traditional modeling approaches address these inhomogeneities either by assigning continuously varying thermal conductivity fields or by using simplified interface models. A common interface model is the Kapitza conductance framework~\cite{kapitza1941study}, which introduces an effective interfacial thermal conductance, $G_K$, by relating the temperature discontinuity $\Delta T$ across an abrupt interface to the local heat flux via $j = -G_K \Delta T$.


While highly effective for macroscopic and near-equilibrium conditions, classical heat conduction models based on Fourier thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) and Kapitza interfacial thermal conductance ($G_\text{K}$) break down in nanoscale materials and ultrafast thermal regimes. A growing body of experimental evidence has revealed pronounced non-Fourier behavior, including wave-like heat propagation (second sound)~\cite{ackerman1966second,mcnelly1970heat,jackson1970second,pohl1976observation,narayanamurti1972observation,danil1979observation,huberman2019observation,ding2022observation,jeong2021transient,beardo2021observation}, quasi-ballistic transport~\cite{maznev2011onset,minnich2011thermal,johnson2013direct,johnson2015non,hua2019generalized,beardo2021general}, and signatures of phonon Poiseuille flow~\cite{machida2018observation,markov2018hydrodynamic,martelli2018thermal,machida2020phonon,huang2023observation,huang2024graphite}. These observations highlight the essential roles of temporal memory and spatial nonlocality, fundamentally incompatible with purely diffusive descriptions.

In response to these observations, a variety of generalized transport models have been developed to extend the classical framework. Notably, the Maxwell–Cattaneo–Vernotte (MCV)~\cite{maxwell1866dynamical,cattaneo1948atti,vernotte1958paradoxes,chester1963second} and Guyer–Krumhansl (GK)~\cite{guyer1966solution,guyer1966thermal,joseph1989heat} equations incorporate finite relaxation times for transient heat flux and higher-order spatial gradients of inhomogeneous flux, respectively, to account for memory and nonlocal effects. While these models formally extend Fourier’s law into the ultrafast and nanoscale regimes, they typically rely on the phenomenological introduction of additional transport parameters, such as flux relaxation time $\tau$, nonlocal length scale $l$, or phonon viscosity~\cite{simoncelli2020generalization}, to complement classical quantities like thermal conductivity and interfacial conductance. 

However, due to the absence of quantitative definitions grounded in microscopic theory, these non-Fourier parameters are often treated as fitting variables rather than as rigorously derived properties. As a result, their predictive capacity remains limited, and empirical calibration is generally required for each specific material system or device geometry.

Microscopically, the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) provides a quantitative framework for modeling heat conduction from first principles. Numerical solutions of the linearized BTE~\cite{hua2020space,chiloyan2021green,malviya2025efficient} have revealed pronounced deviations from Fourier behavior, particularly under cryogenic conditions and in low-dimensional or nanostructured materials. These deviations are often further exacerbated in heterogeneous systems, where spatial variations in structure and composition enhance gradients in local temperature and heat flux fields. Despite its theoretical rigor, BTE-based modeling becomes computationally prohibitive for strongly inhomogeneous phonon systems and may obscure the physical mechanisms underlying non-Fourier thermal transport. As a result, a conceptual and practical divide remains between atomistic simulations and continuum-scale modeling and measurements.

% Despite decades of progress in thermal transport modeling, a central question remains: Can memory, spatial nonlocality, and material inhomogeneity in heat conduction be derived systematically from microscopic dynamics without resorting to phenomenological assumptions? Existing frameworks, including extensions of the Boltzmann transport equation, often treat these effects heuristically or require empirical calibration.
In this work, we perform a first-principles statistical analysis of phonon dynamics to rigorously establish the connection between microscopic degrees of freedom and macroscopic heat transport behavior. Building on the projection-operator formalism~\cite{zwanzig1960ensemble,zwanzig1961memory,zwanzig2001nonequilibrium}, we adopt Zwanzig’s framework for irreversible processes, which systematically separates slow thermodynamic variables, such as temperature, from fast \textit{irrelevant} microscopic modes. This separation naturally introduces temporal memory and spatial nonlocality through the coupled dynamics of the \textit{irrelevant} degrees of freedom, components traditionally treated as stochastic noise, but shown here to play a central role in governing heat conduction in nonuniform media.

Our earlier formulation~\cite{crawford2024theory} addressed transient, local heat conduction in homogeneous media using a time-domain memory kernel function, $\overleftrightarrow{Z}(t)$. In the present work, we extend this framework to incorporate both spatial nonlocality and material inhomogeneity. Rather than relying on phenomenological extensions of classical transport models, we derive the governing equations directly from microscopic dynamics in terms of a spatiotemporal kernel function, $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$, which provides a rigorous statistical foundation for capturing temporal memory, spatial nonlocality, and interfacial heat conduction in heterogeneous media across a broad spectrum of transport regimes.

Crucially, the resulting unified theory captures a wide range of non-Fourier phenomena, including second sound and Poiseuille flow, within a single statistical formalism. In appropriate limits, it recovers established models such as Fourier’s law, the empirical MCV equation, and the hydrodynamic GK equation. Moreover, the transport descriptors introduced here can be computed from atomistic simulations, enabling predictive modeling of heat transport in complex, nanoscale, and compositionally nonuniform systems.

\section{Statistical Theory of Phonon-Mediated Heat Conduction}
\label{sec:phonon_conduction}
\subsection{Zwanzig Projection} \label{sec:zwanzig}
The nonequilibrium statistical framework adopted in this study, originally proposed by Zwanzig~\cite{zwanzig1960ensemble,zwanzig1961memory}, provides a systematic projection-operator approach for modeling irreversible processes. This formalism partitions the full set of microscopic state variables into two distinct categories: (i) a small subset of slowly evolving, coarse-grained \textit{relevant} variables that govern macroscopic transport, and (ii) a large ensemble of rapidly fluctuating \textit{irrelevant} variables that encode microscopic dissipation and thermal noise. Within this framework, the evolution of relevant variables is statistically influenced by the dynamics of irrelevant ones, leading to non-Markovian, memory-dependent behavior as an emergent feature of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics~\cite{zwanzig2001nonequilibrium}. A summary of the Zwanzig projection formalism, using notation consistent with this work, is provided in Appendix~\ref{app:projection}.

%This assumption becomes increasingly uncertain in ultrafast or nanoscale regimes, where the spatial and temporal averaging required for temperature inference may no longer be valid. 
In the context of heat conduction, the temperature field $T(\vec{r}, t)$ is identified as the primary relevant variable governing macroscopic energy transport. While temperature is rigorously defined in thermodynamic equilibrium, its extension to nonequilibrium systems relies on the assumption of local thermal equilibrium. Experimentally, $T(\vec{r}, t)$ is typically inferred from spatially and temporally resolved observables—such as thermal expansion, Raman shifts, or optical reflectance—which are calibrated under equilibrium conditions and interpreted as proxies for temperature. Consequently, the validity of $T(\vec{r}, t)$ as a well-defined thermodynamic field becomes increasingly uncertain in ultrafast or nanoscale regimes, where the assumption of local equilibrium may fail to capture the full complexity of nonequilibrium states. The limitations and implications of this assumption are discussed further in Appendix~\ref{app:local_thermal_eq}.

The macroscopic heat flux $\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)$ is another central quantity in thermal transport, yet it cannot be directly measured. Instead, it is typically inferred from the evolution of the temperature field via the energy conservation relation in Eq.~\eqref{eq:conservation}. As a result, theories of heat conduction treat $T(\vec{r}, t)$ as the sole independent relevant variable, while $\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)$ is regarded as a dependent macroscopic quantity that emerges from the underlying microscopic dynamics. A complementary transport equation is therefore required to describe how the transient heat flux field $\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)$ responds to nonequilibrium conditions in the material medium.

Our statistical analysis begins by considering heat conduction in an infinitely large, homogeneous vibrating lattice, which can be accurately described using the phonon gas model. In this model, thermal excitations are characterized by the occupation numbers of vibrational modes. For convenience, each phonon mode is indexed by a composite label $\alpha = (\vec{q}, b)$, where $\vec{q}$ denotes the wavevector and $b$ indicates the phonon branch. The set of local occupation numbers $\{ n_\alpha(\vec{r}, t) \}$ defines the microscopic state of the system, from which macroscopic quantities such as local energy density and heat flux can be constructed as:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:phonon}    
\begin{eqnarray}
    e(\vec{r},t) &= \frac{1}{V} \sum_{\alpha} n_\alpha(\vec{r},t) \hbar \omega_\alpha,\\ 
   \vec{j}(\vec{r},t) &= \frac{1}{V} \sum_{\alpha} n_\alpha(\vec{r},t) \hbar \omega_\alpha \vec{v}_\alpha,
\end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}
where $\omega_\alpha$ and $\vec{v}_\alpha$ are the angular frequency and group velocity of phonon mode $\alpha$, respectively, and $V$ is the system volume.

To analyze microscopic dynamics of a phonon gas, we consider the deviation of phonon occupation numbers from equilibrium: $\delta n_\alpha(\vec{r}, t) = n_\alpha(\vec{r}, t) - n^{\mathrm{eq}}_\alpha(T_0)$, where $n^{\mathrm{eq}}_\alpha(T_0)$ denotes the equilibrium occupation number of mode $\alpha$ at the global equilibrium temperature $T_0$. In the linear response regime, the evolution of these deviations is governed by the linearized phonon scattering matrix $\mathbb{L}$, whose elements $L_{\alpha\beta}$ are defined in the phonon occupation number representation:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq_lpsm}
\left. \frac{d n_{\alpha}(\vec{r},t)}{d t} \right|_{\text{relax}} \approx - \sum_{\beta} L_{\alpha \beta} \cdot \frac{\sinh \left(\frac{\hbar \omega_{\beta}}{2 k_\mathrm{B} T_0} \right)}{\sinh \left(\frac{\hbar \omega_{\alpha}}{2 k_\mathrm{B} T_0} \right)} \cdot \left[n_{\beta}(\vec{r}, t) - n^{\mathrm{eq}}_{\beta}(T_0)\right].
\end{equation}

The linearized scattering operator $\mathbb{L}$ is a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix that encodes phonon-mode-specific relaxation rates and inter-phonon-mode couplings, forming the foundation for the eigenmode decomposition central to our theoretical framework. Owing to the symmetry of phonon occupation numbers under wavevector inversion ($\vec{q} \leftrightarrow -\vec{q}$), the eigenmodes of $\mathbb{L}$ can be classified by their parity. Odd-parity modes, which are antisymmetric under $\vec{q}$ inversion, contribute directly to the net heat flux, whereas even-parity modes represent $\vec{q}$-space symmetric deviations that do not carry net energy current. The complete orthonormal set of eigenvectors includes a single zero-eigenvalue Bose–Einstein mode, along with a hierarchy of even-parity modes $\nu_\iota$ and odd-parity modes $\mu_\lambda$:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:eigenmodes}
\begin{eqnarray}
\sum_{\alpha} L_{\alpha \beta} c^{1/2}_\beta &=& 0, \quad\text{(Bose–Einstein mode)} \\
\sum_{\alpha} L_{\alpha \beta} \nu_{\iota\beta} &=& \varepsilon_{\iota} \nu_{\iota\alpha}, \quad\text{(even parity)} \\
\sum_{\alpha} L_{\alpha \beta} \mu_{\lambda\beta} &=& \gamma_{\lambda} \mu_{\lambda\alpha}. \quad\text{(odd parity)}
\end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}

These eigenmodes serve as a physically meaningful, orthonormal basis to describe the nonequilibrium phonon distribution. The odd-parity modes govern heat flux, while the even-parity modes encode residual deviations from local equilibrium. This basis allows a compact representation of microscopic dynamics and connects directly to macroscopic observables. The parity of each eigenmode is defined by its symmetry under wavevector inversion in reciprocal space. The eigenvectors $\vec{w}$ (Bose–Einstein mode), $\{\vec{\nu}_\iota\}$ (even parity), and $\{\vec{\mu}_\lambda\}$ (odd parity) form a complete orthonormal basis spanning the space of phonon occupation number fluctuations. The indices $\iota = 1, \dots, M_\mathrm{E}$ and $\lambda = 1, \dots, M_\mathrm{O}$ denote the even and odd parity modes, respectively. Including the zero-eigenvalue Bose–Einstein mode, the completeness condition reads $1 + M_\mathrm{E} + M_\mathrm{O} = N_\mathrm{mode}$.

Within the Zwanzig formalism, the Bose–Einstein mode with zero eigenvalue corresponds to the local energy density, with its normalized eigenvector given by $w_\alpha = \left(c_\alpha / C\right)^{1/2}$, where $C = \sum_{\alpha} c_\alpha$ denotes the total heat capacity of the phonon gas. The mode amplitude of this Bose–Einstein mode is proportional to the temperature field $T(\vec{r}, t)$, which serves as the sole independent relevant variable governing macroscopic heat transport. The eigenvalues $\varepsilon_\iota > 0$ and $\gamma_\lambda \geq 0$ characterize the relaxation rates of the irrelevant variables associated with the even- and odd-parity modes, respectively.

Using this orthonormal basis, the nonequilibirum deviation of the phonon occupation number from equilibrium can be expressed as:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:mode_n}
\begin{split}
n_\alpha(\vec{r}, t) = n^{\mathrm{eq}}_\alpha(T_0) + 
\frac{
\left( \frac{c_\alpha}{k_\mathrm{B}} \right)^{1/2} \frac{T(\vec{r}, t) - T_0}{T_0} 
+ \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_\mathrm{E}} \nu_{\iota\alpha} \theta_\iota(\vec{r}, t) 
+ \sum_{\lambda=1}^{M_\mathrm{O}} \mu_{\lambda\alpha} \eta_\lambda(\vec{r}, t)
}{2\sinh\left( \frac{\hbar \omega_\alpha}{2k_\mathrm{B} T_0} \right)}.
\end{split}
\end{equation}

Conversely, the Zwanzig variables of phonon heat conduction, $T(\vec{r}, t)$, $\theta_\iota(\vec{r}, t)$, and $\eta_\lambda(\vec{r}, t)$, can be projected from $n_\alpha(\vec{r}, t)$ using:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:OP}
 \begin{eqnarray}
&T(\vec{r},t) =& T_{0} + \frac{1}{C} \sum_{\alpha =1}^{N_{\mathrm{mode}}}  \left[ n_{\alpha}(\vec{r},t) - n^{\mathrm{eq}}_{\alpha}(T_{0}) \right] \cdot \hbar \omega_{\alpha}, \label{eq:OP_local_T} \\
&\theta_{\iota}(\vec{r},t) =& \sum_{\alpha =1}^{N_{\mathrm{mode}}} 2 \sinh\left(\frac{\hbar \omega_{\alpha}}{2 k_\mathrm{B} T_0}\right)  \cdot \left[ n_{\alpha}(\vec{r},t) - n^{\mathrm{eq}}_{\alpha}(T_{0}) \right] \cdot \nu_{\iota \alpha}, \label{eq:OP_E} \\
&\eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r},t) =& \sum_{\alpha =1}^{N_{\mathrm{mode}}} 2 \sinh\left(\frac{\hbar \omega_{\alpha}}{2 k_\mathrm{B} T_0}\right) \cdot \left[ n_{\alpha}(\vec{r},t) - n^{\mathrm{eq}}_{\alpha}(T_{0}) \right] \cdot \mu_{\lambda \alpha}. \label{eq:OP_O}
 \end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}
The variables $\eta_{\lambda}$ and $\theta_{\iota}$ represent projections of the phonon distribution onto the odd- and even-parity eigenmodes of the scattering operator, respectively. 

The odd-parity variables $\eta_{\lambda}$ encode the microscopic fluctuations associated with net energy flow and are responsible for carrying the macroscopic heat flux. Specifically, the total heat flux can be reconstructed as a linear superposition of these flux-mode amplitudes:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:flux}
\vec{j}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{V} \sum_{\lambda =1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \vec{j}_\lambda(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{V} \sum_{\lambda =1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \vec{\Lambda}(\lambda) \cdot \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r},t),
\end{equation}
where the vector $\vec{\Lambda}(\lambda)$ is defined as
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eigenmode_Lambda}
\vec{\Lambda}(\lambda) = \sum_{\alpha =1}^{N_{\mathrm{mode}}} \frac{\mu_{\lambda \alpha} \hbar \omega_{\alpha} \vec{v}_{\alpha}}{2 \sinh(\hbar \omega_{\alpha}/2 k_\text{B} T_{0})} 
= k_\text{B}^{1/2} T_0 \sum_{\alpha =1}^{N_{\mathrm{mode}}} c_{\alpha}^{1/2} \mu_{\lambda \alpha} \vec{v}_{\alpha},
\end{equation}
and quantifies the contribution of the odd-parity mode $\eta_\lambda$ to the corresponding modal heat flux $\vec{j}_\lambda$.

The even-parity eigenmodes $\theta_{\iota}$ are orthogonal to both the equilibrium Bose–Einstein mode and the flux-carrying odd-parity modes. While they do not directly contribute to the macroscopic heat flux $\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)$, they play a crucial indirect role by mediating the coupling between different flux modes in space and time. These variables encode residual deviations from local equilibrium and govern how microscopic memory and spatial correlations influence the evolution of the heat flux. Their rapid relaxation, characterized by eigenvalues $\varepsilon_\iota > 0$, modulates the dynamic response of $\eta_\lambda$ and enables nonlocal effects to emerge systematically in the reduced-order transport equations. Together, $\theta_\iota$ and $\eta_\lambda$ define the irreversibly relaxing subspace that underpins a unified theory of heat conduction beyond the classical paradigm.

\subsection{Zwanzig Dynamics}
\label{sec:model-coupled dynamics}
Within the Zwanzig projection formalism, we construct the mode-coupled dynamics by expressing the projected variables in terms of the eigenmodes of the scattering operator $\mathbb{L}$ and derive a hierarchy of transport equations that underpins our theory. This formulation begins with the evolution equation for the mode-resolved phonon occupation numbers $n_\alpha(\vec{r}, t)$, governed by the linearized Boltzmann transport equation (td-phBTE):
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bte_phonon_mode}
\frac{\partial n_{\alpha}(\vec{r},t)}{\partial t} +  \vec{v}_{\alpha}(\vec{r}) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} n_{\alpha}(\vec{r}, t) =- \sum_{\beta =1}^{N_{\mathrm{mode}}} L_{\alpha \beta}(\vec{r}) \frac{\sinh(\hbar \omega_{\beta}(\vec{r}) / 2 k_\text{B} T_0)}{\sinh(\hbar \omega_{\alpha} (\vec{r})/ 2 k_\text{B} T_0)} \left( n_{\beta}(\vec{r},t) - n^{\mathrm{eq}}_{\beta}(T_0) \right).
\end{equation}

As detailed in Appendix~\ref{app:math_detail}, Eq.~\eqref{eq:bte_phonon_mode} can be reformulated as a coupled system of equations involving three sets of variables: \begin{itemize}
    \item the independent \textit{relevant} variable $T(\vec{r}, t)$,
    \item the flux-carrying odd-parity \textit{irrelevant} variables $\eta_\lambda(\vec{r}, t)$, and
    \item the nonlocal even-parity \textit{irrelevant} variables $\theta_\iota(\vec{r}, t)$.
\end{itemize}

To demonstrate how the mode-coupled transport equations specialize under different physical conditions, we consider two limiting cases: perfectly homogeneous phonon gases and spatially varying inhomogeneous systems.
\subsubsection{Homogeneous Phonon Gases}
\label{sec:homogeneous_phono}
We begin by considering an infinitely large and defect-free crystal in which phonon–phonon scattering arises solely from lattice anharmonicity. As a result, all phonon properties, including mode frequency $\omega$, group velocity $\vec{v}$, and the phonon scattering matrix $\mathbb{L}$, are spatially homogeneous and independent of position $\vec{r}$. Under these conditions, the coupled system of equations takes the following form:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:bte_eigen}
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:bte_T}
C \cdot \frac{\partial T(\vec{r},t)}{\partial t} &=& - \sum_{\lambda =1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \vec{\Lambda}(\lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \eta_{\lambda} (\vec{r}, t), \\
\label{eq:bte_O}
\frac{\partial \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r},t)}{\partial t} + \gamma_{\lambda} \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r},t) &=& - \frac{1}{k_\text{B} T_0^2} \vec{\Lambda}(\lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}, t) - \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_{\text{E}}} \vec{\Pi} (\lambda , \iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \theta_{\iota} (\vec{r},t), \\
\label{eq:bte_E}
\frac{\partial \theta_{\iota}(\vec{r},t)}{\partial t} + \varepsilon_{\iota} \theta_{\iota}(\vec{r},t) &=& -\sum_{\lambda=1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \vec{\Pi}(\lambda , \iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \eta_{\lambda} (\vec{r},t).
\end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}
Here, Eq.~(\ref{eq:bte_T}) corresponds directly to the energy conservation relation given in Eq.~(\ref{eq:conservation}), using the definition of the heat flux in terms of the flux-mode variables as introduced in Eq.~(\ref{eq:flux}). The gradient terms in Eqs.~(\ref{eq:bte_O}) and (\ref{eq:bte_E}) couple irrelevant variables of opposite parity, with the coupling coefficient between the $\lambda$-th flux mode and the $\iota$-th nonlocal mode defined as:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:coupling_coefficients}
\vec{\Pi} (\lambda , \iota) \equiv \sum_{\alpha = 1}^{N_{\mathrm{mode}}} \mu_{\lambda \alpha} \nu_{\iota \alpha} \vec{v}_{\alpha}.
\end{equation}
where $\mu_{\lambda \alpha}$ and $\nu_{\iota \alpha}$ are the components of the eigenvectors of the operator $\mathcal{L}$ corresponding to the flux and nonlocal modes, respectively.

Although structurally similar to the mode-resolved phonon transport equations developed by Hua and Lindsay~\cite{hua2020space}, our formulation is derived entirely within the Zwanzig projection framework, yielding a more transparent physical interpretation. Unlike reciprocal-space approaches that rely on Fourier transformation, we construct our solution directly in real space and time, preserving spatial inhomogeneity and enabling hierarchical solution strategies based on modal relaxation times and spatial derivatives. As detailed in Appendix~\ref{app:math_detail}, the flux-mode and nonlocal-mode variables, $\eta_\lambda$ and $\theta_\iota$, emerge naturally from this framework and are obtained in closed form through systematic iterative substitution:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:ana2}
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:ana_2a}
\eta_\lambda(\vec{r}, t) &=& - \int_{0}^{\infty} dt_1 \frac{e^{-\gamma_{\lambda}t_1}}{k_\text{B} T_0^2} \vec{\Lambda}(\lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}, t-t_1) \nonumber \\
&& - \int_{0}^{\infty} dt_1 \, e^{-\gamma_{\lambda}t_1} \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_{\text{E}}} \vec{\Pi}(\lambda , \iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \theta_\iota(\vec{r}, t-t_1), \\
\label{eq:ana_2b}
\theta_{\iota}(\vec{r}, t) &=& - \int_{0}^{\infty} dt_1 \, e^{-\varepsilon_\iota t_1} \sum_{\lambda=1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \vec{\Pi}(\lambda, \iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r}, t-t_1).
\end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}

These expressions highlight the central structure of the Zwanzig-based theory, in which the temperature field acts as the sole independent relevant variable, while all nonequilibrium flux and nonlocal responses emerge from the time-retarded dynamics of rapidly relaxing modal variables. The convolution structure of Eqs.~\eqref{eq:ana2} will be the basis for deriving hierarchical solutions and reduced-order models in the next subsection.
To quantify the influence of nonlocal modes, $\theta_\iota(\vec{r}, t)$, on the macroscopic heat flux $\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)$, we substitute Eq.~(\ref{eq:ana_2b}) into Eq.~(\ref{eq:ana_2a}), which yields a closed-form expression for the flux-mode variables $\eta_\lambda(\vec{r}, t)$:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:flux-mode-only}
\begin{split}
\eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r}, t) &= -\int_{0}^{\infty} dt_1 \frac{e^{-\gamma_\lambda t_1}}{k_\text{B} T^{2}_0} \vec{\Lambda} (\lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r} , t-t_1) \\
& \quad + \int_{0}^{\infty} dt_1 e^{-\gamma_\lambda t_1} \sum_{\lambda'=1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \int_{0}^{\infty} dt_2  \sum_{I,J=1}^{3} \phi_{IJ}(t_2; \lambda, \lambda') \frac{\partial^2 \eta_{\lambda'} (\vec{r}, t-t_1-t_2)}{\partial x_I \partial x_J} , 
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where flux-mode coupling function takes the tensor form: 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:phi}
  \overleftrightarrow{\phi}(t;\lambda, \lambda')=\sum_{\iota=1}^{M_{\text{E}}} 
\vec{\Pi}(\lambda, \iota) \otimes  \vec{\Pi}(\lambda',\iota) ~e^{-{\varepsilon}_{\iota} t}.  
\end{equation}

Equation~\eqref{eq:flux-mode-only} illustrates that the local temperature gradient, $\vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}, t)$, alone does not fully determine the dynamics of the flux-mode variables $\eta_\lambda(\vec{r}, t)$ that govern the macroscopic heat flux $\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)$. In particular, second-order spatial derivatives of $\eta_{\lambda}$, such as $\frac{\partial^2 \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r}, t)}{\partial x_I \partial x_J}$, capture nonlocal nonequilibrium effects that extend beyond the information encoded in $\vec{\nabla}_{r} T$. These higher-order contributions arise from mode-mode coupling and reflect the intrinsic connection between spatial nonlocality and temporal memory in transient heat conduction. A complete description beyond the local equilibrium approximation must account for both effects.

\subsubsection{Inhomogeneous Phonon Gases}
\label{sec:inhomogeneous_phonon}
Real materials consist of finite-sized lattices with surfaces and may exhibit spatial inhomogeneities in atomic structure and composition. When these variations occur gradually in space, without sharp discontinuities, the conventional phonon gas model can be extended to an inhomogeneous phonon framework in which material properties are position-dependent. This scenario is naturally treated by introducing spatially varying harmonic phonon spectra and phonon scattering matrices into the Zwanzig projection formalism, enabling a direct generalization of the homogeneous theory.

For an inhomogeneous phonon gas, we define a position-dependent phonon dispersion and phonon scattering matrix, $\mathcal{L}(\vec{r})$, whose eigenvalues and eigenvectors determine the local auxiliary variables $\eta_\lambda(\vec{r}, t)$ and $\theta_\iota(\vec{r}, t)$. This spatial dependence enables the construction of position-dependent flux-pair factors, $\vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r}; \lambda)$, and nonlocal coupling tensors, $\overleftrightarrow{\Pi}(\vec{r}; \lambda, \iota)$, based on the local phonon spectra and the eigenmodes of the position-dependent scattering matrix $\mathcal{L}(\vec{r})$, following the formulation introduced in Equations ~\eqref{eq:eigenmode_Lambda} and \eqref{eq:coupling_coefficients}.

Further mathematical details of this generalization are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:kernel}. A key result of this extended formulation is that the iterative solution for the flux-mode variables, $\eta_\lambda(\vec{r},t)$, now involves both $\vec{r}$-dependent coefficients, such as $\gamma_\lambda(\vec{r})$ and $\vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda)$,  and an additional first-order spatial derivative term that complements the second-order gradient term present in the homogeneous form given in Eq.~\eqref{eq:flux-mode-only}
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:flux-mode-only_r}
\begin{split}
\eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r}, t) =& -\int_{0}^{\infty} dt_1 \frac{e^{-\gamma_\lambda(\vec{r}) t_1}}{k_\text{B} T^{2}_0} \vec{\Lambda} (\vec{r}; \lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r} , t-t_1) \\
&+ \int_{0}^{\infty} dt_1 e^{-\gamma_\lambda(\vec{r}) t_1} \sum_{\lambda'=1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \int_{0}^{\infty} dt_2 \\
 &\quad \biggr[\sum_{I,J=1}^{3} \Phi_{IJ}(\vec{r},t_2; \lambda, \lambda') \frac{\partial^2 }{\partial x_I \partial x_J} \eta_{\lambda'} (\vec{r}, t-t_1-t_2) \\
 &+  \sum_{I=1}^{3} \psi_I(\vec{r},t_2; \lambda, \lambda') \frac{\partial}{\partial x_I} \eta_{\lambda'} (\vec{r}, t-t_1-t_2) \biggr],
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where the first $\vec{r}$-dependent flux-to-flux coupling function, $\overleftrightarrow{\Phi}$, is defined as
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Phi_r}
  \overleftrightarrow{\Phi}(\vec{r},t;\lambda, \lambda') = \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_{\text{E}}} 
\vec{\Pi}(\vec{r};\lambda, \iota) \otimes  \vec{\Pi}(\vec{r};\lambda',\iota) ~e^{-{\varepsilon}_{\iota}(\vec{r}) t},  
\end{equation}
and corresponds to the spatially varying extension of Eq.~\eqref{eq:phi}. The second $\vec{r}$-dependent nonlocal flux-to-flux coupling function, $\vec{\psi}$, is given by
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:g_r}
  \vec{\psi}(\vec{r},t;\lambda, \lambda') = \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_{\text{E}}} \sum_{J=1}^{3}\Pi_J(\vec{r};\lambda, \iota) \frac{\partial}{\partial x_J} \biggr(\vec{\Pi}(\vec{r};\lambda',\iota) ~e^{-{\varepsilon}_{\iota}(\vec{r}) t} \biggr),  
\end{equation}
and captures additional spatial coupling arising from material heterogeneity in the mode-coupling parameters. Together, these results provide a consistent and extensible foundation for describing nonlocal, transient heat transport across both ideal and complex material systems. They motivate the introduction of a more compact and general representation in terms of space- and time-resolved conduction kernels, developed next.

\section{Reduced Models for Distinct Heat Conduction Regimes}
\label{sec:reduced_models}
Having developed a general expression for phonon-mediated heat flux that accounts for memory effects, spatial nonlocality, and material inhomogeneity in Eq. \eqref{eq:flux-mode-only_r}, we now explore its limiting cases. These include the phonon hydrodynamic regime, the local (transient) regime, the classical diffusive limit, and interfacial conduction. In each case, the full spatiotemporal theory can be systematically reduced to yield simpler yet physically accurate transport models. These reduced forms balance theoretical fidelity with practical feasibility, enabling analytical insight and computational tractability.
\subsection{Hydrodynamic Regime}
\label{sec:phonon_hydrodynamics}
The phonon hydrodynamic regime represents an intermediate transport regime between the ballistic and diffusive limits, where momentum-conserving phonon–phonon scattering dominates over resistive processes. These interactions lead to collective phonon behavior and enable phenomena such as second sound and Poiseuille heat flow. A variety of approximate models, most notably the GK equation, have been developed to describe this regime and to account for a broad range of non-Fourier heat conduction phenomena, including heat wave propagation at cryogenic temperatures and ultrafast time-scales, hydrodynamic heat flux profiles at nanoscales, and anomalous diffusion in nanomaterials.

Within our Zwanzig-based formalism, the hydrodynamic regime emerges naturally when a small subset of odd-parity flux modes exhibits exceptionally slow relaxation. These long-lived modes dominate transient transport and must be retained as macroscopically relevant variables. Their dynamics are coupled to a small number of even-parity (nonlocal) modes, which we treat in a quasi-steady approximation due to their rapid decay.

For clarity, we focus on a crystal with cubic symmetry. In this case, we retain only the three lowest-order flux modes and three corresponding nonlocal modes, while all higher-order degrees of freedom are truncated. The retained flux vectors and coupling tensors are defined as $\vec{\Lambda}_1 = (\Lambda, 0, 0)$, $\vec{\Lambda}_2 = (0, \Lambda, 0)$, $\vec{\Lambda}_3 = (0, 0, \Lambda)$, and $\Pi_K(\lambda,\iota) = \Pi \cdot \delta_{\lambda,K} \cdot \delta_{\iota,K}$. Under these assumptions, the mode-coupled dynamics simplify to:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:bte_php}
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:bte_php_O_first3}
\frac{\partial \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r},t)}{\partial t} + \gamma \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r},t) & \approx & - \frac{\Lambda}{k_\text{B} T_0^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_\lambda} T(\vec{r}, t) - \Pi \frac{\partial}{\partial x_\lambda} \theta_{\lambda} (\vec{r},t), \quad \lambda =1,2,3\\
\label{eq:bte_php_O_others}
\eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r},t) &\approx & 0, \quad \lambda \ge 4\\
\label{eq:bte_php_E_first3}
\theta_{\iota}(\vec{r},t) & \approx& - \varepsilon^{-1} \Pi \frac{\partial}{\partial x_\iota} \eta_{\iota} (\vec{r},t), \quad \iota =1,2,3\\
\label{eq:bte_php_E_others}
\theta_{\iota}(\vec{r},t) &\approx & 0, \quad \iota \ge 4.
\end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}

Combining these relations yields a constitutive law formally equivalent to the GK equation:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:GKE_like}
\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t) = -\kappa\, \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}, t) - \tau\, \frac{\partial \vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)}{\partial t} + l^2 \nabla^2 \vec{j}(\vec{r}, t),
\end{equation}
where $\kappa = \frac{\Lambda^2}{V k_B T_0^2 \gamma}$ is the thermal conductivity, $\tau = \gamma^{-1}$ is the relaxation time, and $l = \frac{\Pi}{\sqrt{\gamma \varepsilon}}$ is the characteristic nonlocal length scale.

The phonon hydrodynamic GK equation treats memory and nonlocality as two distinct non-Fourier effects, with the relaxation time $\tau$ quantifying memory (temporal) effects and the characteristic length scale $l$ capturing spatial nonlocality.  In the limit of negligible nonlocal effects ($l \rightarrow 0$), the GK equation reduces to its temporally nonlocal counterpart, the MCV equation:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:MCV}
\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t) = -\kappa\, \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}, t) - \tau\, \frac{\partial \vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)}{\partial t},
\end{equation}
while in the quasi-steady limit ($\partial \vec{j} / \partial t \approx 0$), it reduces to a nonlocal diffusion equation:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:GKE_diffusion}
\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t) = -\kappa\, \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}, t)  + l^2 \nabla^2 \vec{j}(\vec{r}, t),
\end{equation}
highlighting the role of spatially extended interactions in modifying Fourier-like behavior. 

Although widely used, hydrodynamic models like the GK equation rest on idealized assumptions. They assume nearly crystalline purity and dominance of momentum-conserving scattering, restricting their applicability to select materials and temperature regimes. In contrast, the present formalism provides a unified foundation that recovers the GK equation as a limiting case and clarifies its microscopic basis in terms of mode-resolved phonon dynamics.

\subsection{Local Regime}
\label{sec:ultrafast_and_local}
In many bulk or near-homogeneous materials, the coupling between flux and nonlocal modes is weak. When $\vec{\Pi}(\vec{r}; \lambda, \iota) \rightarrow 0$, the general mode-coupled dynamics for \textit{irrelevant} degrees of freedom simplifies to:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:bte_eigen_local}
\begin{align}
\label{eq:bte_O_local}
\frac{\partial \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r}, t)}{\partial t} + \gamma_{\lambda}(\vec{r}) \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r}, t) &\approx - \frac{1}{k_\text{B} T_0^2} \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r}; \lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r}, t), \\
\label{eq:bte_E_local}
\theta_{\iota}(\vec{r}, t) &\approx 0.
\end{align}
\end{subequations}

In this flux-nonlocal decoupled regime, the influence of the nonlocal-mode variables $\theta_{\iota}(\vec{r}, t)$ on the \textit{relevant} temperature field $T(\vec{r}, t)$ is negligible. This follows directly from the absence of coupling between the \textit{irrelevant} flux modes $\eta_{\lambda}$ and \textit{irrelevant} nonlocal modes $\theta_{\iota}$.

We refer to this limit as the regime of \textit{local} heat conduction, characteristic of bulk or nearly homogeneous materials. Our prior work~\cite{crawford2024theory} analyzed this regime for an infinite, homogeneous phonon gas, capturing both ultrafast transients and the steady-state limit. Here, we extend that formulation to finite and inhomogeneous systems by introducing a position-resolved Zwanzig conduction function, $\overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},t)$, defined as:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Z_t_r}
\overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{V k_\text{B} T_0^2} \sum_{\lambda =1}^{M_\text{O}} \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda) \otimes \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda) e^{-\gamma_\lambda(\vec{r}) t}.
\end{equation}
In this regime, the macroscopic heat flux $\vec{j}(\vec{r},t)$ is approximated as
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:j_local_convolution}
\vec{j}(\vec{r},t) \approx \vec{j}^\text{local}(\vec{r},t) = - \int_{0}^{\infty} dt'\, \overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},t') \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r}, t - t').
\end{equation}

The time dependence of $\overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},t)$ captures intrinsic memory effects associated with ultrafast thermal transport, providing a microscopic foundation for modeling second sound phenomena~\cite{crawford2024theory}. A simplified representation of this kernel function is to approximate it as a single-exponential decay in the time domain:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Z_mvc}
\overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},t) \approx \overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},0)\, e^{-t/\tau(\vec{r})},
\end{equation}
which leads to the MCV equation form of the constitutive relation:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:j_mcv}
\vec{j}(\vec{r},t) = -\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}(\vec{r}) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r},t) - \tau(\vec{r})\, \frac{\partial \vec{j}(\vec{r},t)}{\partial t},
\end{equation}
where the local thermal conductivity tensor is given by $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}(\vec{r}) = \tau(\vec{r})\, \overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},0)$.

In the steady-state limit, Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_local_convolution} reduces to the conventional Fourier’s law, as expressed in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Fourier_law}, where the bulk thermal conductivity tensor $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}(\vec{r})$ is given by:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kappa_local}
\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}(\vec{r}) = \int_{0}^{\infty} dt\, \overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{V k_\text{B} T_0^2} \sum_{\lambda=1}^{M_\text{O}} \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda) \otimes \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda) \gamma_\lambda^{-1}(\vec{r}).
\end{equation}

The commonly observed size dependence of effective thermal conductivity in nanomaterials can be understood as a consequence of spatial variation in the Zwanzig conduction function $\overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r}, t)$, which arises from the position dependence of the phonon spectra and scattering matrix $\mathcal{L}(\vec{r})$. In such systems, structural inhomogeneity, boundary conditions, or geometric confinement may induce spatial variation in the local thermal conductivity tensor $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}(\vec{r})$, encoded through $\gamma_\lambda(\vec{r})$ and $\vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda)$. A particularly notable example is Poiseuille heat flow \cite{sussmann1963thermal}, characterized by a parabolic flux profile and commonly attributed to nonlocal thermal transport. However, as suggested by Eqs.~\eqref{eq:Fourier_law} and \eqref{eq:kappa_local}, such behavior can also emerge from spatially varying local transport properties alone. This underscores the need to distinguish intrinsic spatial nonlocality from nonlocal effects that arise due to spatial inhomogeneity, particularly in nanoscale and nonuniform materials.

\subsection{Diffusive Limit}
\label{sec:steady}
The classical theory of heat conduction applies in the diffusive limit, under the assumptions of bulk and quasi-homogeneous materials operating at quasi-steady-state conditions. In this regime, heat transport is well described by Fourier’s law, Eq. \eqref{eq:Fourier_law}, in which the bulk thermal conductivity tensor $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}$ encapsulates all internal heat dissipation mechanisms. However, at an abrupt material interface, the continuum framework becomes insufficient and must be augmented by an interfacial boundary condition that captures cross-interface heat transfer. A widely used macroscopic formalism introduces the Kapitza (thermal boundary) conductance, $G_{\mathrm{K}}$, through the relation $j_{\mathrm{interface}} = - G_{\mathrm{K}} \Delta T$, where $\Delta T$ is the finite temperature discontinuity across the interface. 

In the remainder of this subsection, we examine heat conduction in the diffusion limit under steady-state conditions, while incorporating more realistic features such as spatial inhomogeneity and nanoscale nonlocal effects. Starting from the general transient Zwanzig equations, we derive a reduced steady-state formulation for the coupled-mode dynamics in inhomogeneous systems:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bte_OE_r_ss}
\begin{cases}
\eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r})  \approx  - \frac{\gamma_{\lambda}^{-1}(\vec{r})}{k_\text{B} T_0^2} \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}) - \gamma_{\lambda}^{-1}(\vec{r}) \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_{\text{E}}} \vec{\Pi} (\vec{r}; \lambda , \iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \theta_{\iota} (\vec{r}),\\
\quad \\
\theta_{\iota}(\vec{r})  \approx  - \varepsilon_{\iota}^{-1}(\vec{r})\sum_{\lambda=1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \vec{\Pi}(\vec{r}; \lambda , \iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \eta_{\lambda} (\vec{r}), 
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
which can be equivalently rewritten in terms of $\eta_\lambda(\vec{r})$ only:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bte_eta_only_r_ss}
\begin{split}
    \eta_{\lambda}(\vec{r})  \approx  & - \frac{\gamma_{\lambda}^{-1}(\vec{r})}{k_\text{B} T_0^2} \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} T(\vec{r}) \\ 
    & + \gamma_{\lambda}^{-1}(\vec{r}) \sum_{\lambda'=1}^{M_{\text{O}}} \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_{\text{E}}} \vec{\Pi} (\vec{r}; \lambda , \iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \biggr[  \varepsilon_{\iota}^{-1}(\vec{r})\vec{\Pi}(\vec{r}; \lambda' , \iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_{r} \eta_{\lambda'} (\vec{r})\biggr].     
\end{split}
\end{equation}

\subsubsection{Hierarchy of Nonlocality}
\label{sec:iterative}
Equation~\eqref{eq:bte_OE_r_ss} reveals an intrinsic hierarchical structure in the mode-resolved dynamics of $\eta_\lambda(\vec{r}, t)$, which admits an iterative expansion. A detailed mathematical derivation of this expansion is provided in Appendix~\ref{app:iterative_solution}.

The zeroth-order solution, $\eta^{(0)}_\lambda(\vec{r})$, is given by
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eta0_ss}
\eta^{(0)}_\lambda (\vec{r}) = - \frac{\gamma_\lambda^{-1}(\vec{r})}{k_B T_0^2}  \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda) \cdot\vec{\nabla}_{r}T(\vec{r}),
\end{equation}
and corresponds to the local conduction regime. It recovers the conventional form of Fourier’s law given in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Fourier_law}, with the thermal conductivity $\kappa$ defined as in Eq.~\eqref{eq:kappa_local}.

Correspondingly, all higher-order correction terms, $\Delta \eta^{(1)}_\lambda, \Delta \eta^{(2)}_\lambda, \dots$, represent nonlocal contributions to the heat flux that are absent in the classical Fourier description. These corrections can be systematically computed from the microscopic inputs, including the harmonic phonon spectra and the local phonon scattering properties. Specifically, nonlocality is governed by mode-specific relaxation rates, $\gamma_\lambda$ and $\varepsilon_\iota$, the mode–flux coupling vectors, $\vec{\Lambda}$, and the flux–nonlocal mode coupling tensors, $\vec{\Pi}$. As an example, substituting the zeroth-order solution from Eq.~\eqref{eq:eta0_ss} into the second term on the right-hand side of Eq.~\eqref{eq:bte_eta_only_r_ss} yields the first-order correction $\Delta \eta^{(1)}_\lambda$:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eta1_ss}
\begin{split}
    \Delta \eta^{(1)}_\lambda (\vec{r})  =  -  \frac{\gamma_\lambda^{-1}(\vec{r})}{k_B T^2_0} \biggr[ &\delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r};\lambda) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) + \sum_{J_1=1}^{3} \delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r};\lambda, J_1) \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{J_1}} \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) \\
    &+ \sum_{J_1,J_2=1}^{3}  \delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r};\lambda, J_1, J_2) \cdot 
    \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial x_{J_1} \partial x_{J_2}}  \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) \biggr],
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where 
\begin{subequations}
    \begin{eqnarray}
        \delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r};\lambda) &=& \sum_{\lambda'=1}^{M_\text{O}} \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_\text{E}} \big( \vec{\Pi}(\vec{r};\lambda,\iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r\big) \big[ \varepsilon_\iota^{-1}(\vec{r}) \gamma_{\lambda'}^{-1}(\vec{r}) \big(\vec{\Pi}(\vec{r};\lambda',\iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r \big) \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda')\big], \label{eq:c1_0}\\
        %
        \delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r};\lambda,J_1)& =& \sum_{\lambda'=1}^{M_\text{O}} \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_\text{E}}\big[ \big( \vec{\Pi}(\vec{r};\lambda,\iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r\big) ~ \Pi_{J_1}(\vec{r};\lambda',\iota) \varepsilon_\iota^{-1}(\vec{r}) \gamma_{\lambda'}^{-1}(\vec{r}) \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda')\big]  \nonumber \\
        & +&\big[ \big( \vec{\Pi}(\vec{r};\lambda,\iota) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r\big)  \Pi_{J_1}(\vec{r};\lambda',\iota)\big] \varepsilon_\iota^{-1}(\vec{r}) \gamma_{\lambda'}^{-1}(\vec{r}) \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda'),\label{eq:c1_1}\\
        %
        \delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r};\lambda,J_1,J_2) &=& \sum_{\lambda'=1}^{M_\text{O}} \sum_{\iota=1}^{M_\text{E}}  \Pi_{J_1}(\vec{r};\lambda,\iota) \Pi_{J_2}(\vec{r};\lambda',\iota) \varepsilon_\iota^{-1}(\vec{r}) \gamma_{\lambda'}^{-1}(\vec{r}) \vec{\Lambda}(\vec{r};\lambda').\label{eq:c1_2}
    \end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}

Specifically, the first-order correction term $\Delta \eta^{(1)}_\lambda$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:eta1_ss} reveals that nonlocal heat conduction arises from flux responses to higher-order spatial derivatives of the local temperature gradient field, $\vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r})$. The leading-order nonlocal corrections involve second derivatives of the form $\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_{J_1} \partial x_{J_2}} \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r})$, whose corresponding coefficients $\delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r}; \lambda, J_1, J_2)$, defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:c1_2}, depend on weighted products of the flux–nonlocal mode coupling tensors $\vec{\Pi}$ and the inverse relaxation rates. These terms reflect spatial coupling between flux-carrying and nonlocal modes, and their magnitude becomes appreciable when both types of modes are long-lived and strongly coupled. Interestingly, the lower-order coefficients $\delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r}; \lambda)$ and $\delta \vec{c}^{(1)}(\vec{r}; \lambda, J_1)$, given in Eqs.~\eqref{eq:c1_0} and \eqref{eq:c1_1}, respectively, vanish in homogeneous media. This observation highlights that nonlocality and spatial inhomogeneity are not independent phenomena but instead arise from a common microscopic mechanism—the coupling between slowly relaxing flux and nonlocal modes.


Similarly, all higher-order correction terms $\Delta \eta^{(n)}_\lambda$ can be expressed as a series involving spatial derivatives of the temperature field up to order $2n$, i.e., terms of the form $\frac{\partial^{(2n)}}{\partial x_{J_1} \partial x_{J_2} \dots \partial x_{J_{2n}}} \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r})$. Consequently, the steady-state heat flux can be written as:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:j_ss_expansion}
\vec{j}(\vec{r}) =  - \sum_{n_1=0}^{\infty} \sum_{n_2=0}^{\infty} \sum_{n_3=0}^{\infty}  \frac{1}{n_1! n_2! n_3!}\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r}; n_1, n_2, n_3) \cdot \frac{\partial^{n_1+n_2+n_3}}{\partial^{n_1} x \partial^{n_2} y  \partial^{n_3} z } \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}),
\end{equation}
where $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r}; n_1, n_2, n_3)$ are referred to in this work as generalized higher-order thermal conductivity tensors.

Within this formalism, all orders of these generalized conductivity tensors for a phonon gas can, in principle, be computed from microscopic phonon properties, given knowledge of the position-dependent phonon dispersion relations and phonon scattering matrix. However, in practical settings, it is often unnecessary to retain the complete series. For many materials and geometries, a finite truncation captures the essential physics while significantly reducing computational cost. The appropriate truncation order depends on the strength of intrinsic nonlocality, the required numerical accuracy, and the spatial resolution of interest in simulations or experiments.

We further demonstrate that in homogeneous media, the generalized thermal conductivity tensors become spatially invariant, i.e., independent of $\vec{r}$, and all odd-order tensors vanish due to symmetry. For isotropic media,  all $n$-th order generalized thermal conductivity tensors $\kappa^{n}(n_1,n_2,n_3)$. Accordingly, the steady-state heat flux reduces to:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:j_ss_iso}
\begin{split}
&\vec{j}_{\text{iso}}(\vec{r}) = - {\kappa}_{\text{iso}}^{(0)} \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{(2n)!}\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(2n)} \nabla^{2n}_r \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) \right) \\
&= - {\kappa}_{\text{iso}}^{(0)} \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r}) + \frac{\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(2)}}{2 \kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(0)}}\nabla^{2}_r \left( -\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(0)} \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2}{(2n+2)!} \frac{\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(2n+2)} \kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(0)}}{\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(2)}} \nabla_r^{2n} \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) \right) \\
& \approx   - {\kappa}_{\text{iso}}^{(0)} \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) + l^2 \nabla^{2}_r \vec{j}_{\text{iso}}(\vec{r}),
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where the characteristic length $l$ is defined as $l = \sqrt{\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(2)} / (2\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(0)})}$. The difference between the two infinite series, namely $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{(2n)!}\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(2n)} \nabla^{2n}_r \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) \right)$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{2}{2(n+1)!} \frac{\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(2n+2)} \kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(0)}}{\kappa_{\text{iso}}^{(2)}} \nabla_r^{2n} \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r}) \right)$, is assumed to be negligible compared to the leading term ${\kappa}^{(0)} \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{r})$, justifying the approximation in the last line.

A comparison between Eqs.~\eqref{eq:GKE_diffusion} and~\eqref{eq:j_ss_iso} reveals that two distinct representations of nonlocal heat conduction, namely the hydrodynamic form based on the $\nabla^{2}_r \vec{j}$ correction and the generalized formulation involving higher-order thermal conductivity tensors $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa^{(n)}}$, are semi-quantitatively consistent. However, the hydrodynamic representation (Eqs.~\eqref{eq:GKE_diffusion} and~\eqref{eq:j_ss_iso})~should be regarded as an approximation to the full tensorial expansion (Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion}).

The concept of an infinite hierarchy of generalized thermal conductivity tensors, as defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion}, aligns closely with the original notion of nonlocal thermal conductivity pioneered by Mahan and Claro~\cite{mahan1988nonlocal}. However, their formulation was restricted to homogeneous phonon systems and focused primarily on the lowest-order correction term, $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}^{(2)}$, which characterizes nonlocal heat flux contributions arising from the second-order spatial derivatives of the temperature gradient field, $\vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r}, t)$. Additionally, their work proposed that the magnitude of nonlocal effects scales with the phonon mean free path, which is a heuristic assumption that has been widely adopted in subsequent discussions of nonlocal transport, often without rigorous justification.

In contrast, our analysis is grounded in a first-principles statistical framework that avoids phenomenological assumptions. In particular, Eq.~\eqref{eq:eta1_ss} reveals that the generalized conductivity tensors $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}^{(n)}$ are not simply functions of phonon mean free paths, but depend intricately on microscopic transport properties. Specifically, these tensors are directly proportional to the fundamental flux–nonlocal-mode coupling coefficients, $\vec{\Pi}$, and inversely proportional to the relaxation rates $\gamma^{-1}$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}$. 

The general formalism expressed in Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion} further indicates that this framework, based on an infinite set of generalized thermal conductivity tensors, is applicable to a wide range of systems beyond phonon-mediated transport, thereby providing a unified approach for characterizing spatially nonlocal thermal phenomena across diverse material platforms.
\subsubsection{Kernel Function Representation}
\label{sec:kernel}
While Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion} provides a general and complete mathematical description of heat conduction in the diffusive limit by using macroscopically measurable generalized transport coefficients, its infinite series form is often cumbersome to implement numerically. To address this, we reformulate the theory using a more compact but mathematically equivalent representation,  using a spatial kernel function formalism to reformulate Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion} as
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:J_ss_kernel_r_R} 
\vec{j}(\vec{r}) = - \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} \overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R}) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_rT(\vec{R}), 
\end{equation}
where $\overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R})$, typically peak at $\vec{r}$ and decays as $\vec{R}$ moves away from $\vec{r}$. The generalized higher order thermal conductivity tensors in Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion} are simply the spatial-moments of the kernel function, $\overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R})$:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:general_kappa} 
\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r};n_1,n_2,n_3) = - \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} \overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R}) {(\delta x)}^{n_1} {(\delta y)}^{n_2} {(\delta z)}^{n_3}.   
\end{equation}

Further details are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:kernel}. The kernel function formalism offers a compact alternative to the generalized tensorial hierarchy by eliminating the need for explicit truncation of higher-order terms. Rather than computing the full series of generalized thermal conductivity tensors, the key physics can be captured by approximating the spatial heat conduction kernel in the diffusive limit, $\overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R})$, using simplified functional forms with a small number of physically meaningful parameters. These kernels encapsulate the complex microscopic behavior of phonon transport and enable efficient modeling of spatially nonlocal effects. As such, the formalism establishes a new paradigm for both numerical evaluation of transport properties and interpretation of experimental observations in  nanoscale regimes.

As an illustrate example, we consider a simple model of a homogeneous and isotropic kernel function $\overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R})$ as:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kernel_gaussian} 
Z_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R}) = \frac{\kappa}{{(\sqrt{2 \pi}a)}^3} e^{-\frac{|\vec{r}-\vec{R}|^2}{2a^2}},
\end{equation}
where $\kappa$ denotes the conventional lattice thermal conductivity, and $a$ represents a characteristic length scale of the medium. Higher-order generalized thermal conductivity coefficients can be computed using Eq.~\eqref{eq:general_kappa}. For instance, in isotropic media, the second-order components satisfy $\kappa^{(2)}(2,0,0) = \kappa^{(2)}(0,2,0) = \kappa^{(2)}(0,0,2) = \kappa a^2$. According to Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_iso}, the characteristic length $a$ used in Eq.~\eqref{eq:kernel_gaussian} corresponds to $\sqrt{2}\,l$, where $l$ is the nonlocal length appearing in the hydrodynamic GK equation. 

Spatial kernel functions have appeared previously in phenomenological models of nonlocal heat conduction, notably in the works of Sobolev~\cite{sobolev19942175} and Allen~\cite{alvarez2018thermal}. In particular, Allen introduced a conceptual example to interpret the nonlinear temperature profiles ubiquitously observed in nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, especially near localized heat sources and sinks, using hypothesized spatial conduction kernels. However, most prior studies treated these kernel functions as empirical fitting tools for experimental or simulation data, without establishing a clear connection to microscopic theory. Notably, earlier kernel-based models often echoed the notion introduced by Mahan and Claro~\cite{mahan1988nonlocal}, suggesting that the characteristic length scale of spatial kernels correlates qualitatively with the phonon mean free path. In many cases, the kernel functions were applied to homogeneous media under the assumption of translational invariance, such that $\overleftrightarrow{Z}_D(\vec{r}, \vec{R})$ depends only on the relative displacement $\vec{R} - \vec{r}$. This allowed the use of Fourier transforms to represent the kernels in reciprocal $\vec{k}$-space, further simplifying the analysis under the assumption of spatial homogeneity.

Grounded in microscopic statistical analysis, our analysis demonstrates the consistency of three representations of spatial nonlocality in the diffusive limit: (i) an approximate form involving second-order spatial derivatives of the heat flux, $\nabla^2 \vec{j}$, as expressed in Eq.~\eqref{eq:GKE_diffusion}; (ii) a systematic series expansion in terms of generalized higher-order thermal conductivity tensors, $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}^{(n)}$, as shown in Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion}; and (iii) an integral formulation using a spatial heat conduction kernel, $\overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r}, \vec{R})$, given in Eq.~\eqref{eq:J_ss_kernel_r_R}. While the first representation provides a simplified hydrodynamic approximation, the latter two offer mathematically rigorous and broadly applicable formulations that accurately capture spatial nonlocality, thereby establishing a robust framework for modeling nanoscale and spatially heterogeneous thermal transport. Importantly, our analysis provides a microscopic foundation for numerically evaluating the full series of generalized thermal conductivity tensors and links them to the spatial kernel function through well-defined mathematical moment relations.

\subsubsection{Interfacial Heat Conduction}
\label{sec:kapitza}
An important feature of the spatial kernel function formalism presented in Eq.~\eqref{eq:J_ss_kernel_r_R} is its universality for nonuniform media including both inhomogeneous materials with varying compositions and finite dimensions heterogeneous materials featuring sharply defined interfaces, where temperature gradients may become discontinuous across the interface. The explicit interfacial temperature jumps observed in experiment are traditionally described by the Kapitza model of interfacial heat conduction:


To apply the spatial conduction kernel function presented earlier, we consider that in addition to the conventional finite gradient field $\vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r},t)$ defined in the bulk, the interfacial contribution to the temperature gradient can be expressed using a $\delta$-function formalism:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:delta_function_gradent}
\vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r},t) = \Delta T(\vec{r}_\text{AB},t) ~\delta(\vec{r} - \vec{r}_\text{AB}).
\end{equation}

Using Eq.~\eqref{eq:delta_function_gradent}, we generalize Eq.~\eqref{eq:J_ss_kernel_r_R} to account explicitly for the contributions of abrupt interfaces in two cases. For $\vec{r}$ located within the bulk regions $\mathbb{V}$ of either material \textit{A} or \textit{B}, we have:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:j_ss_with_interface}
\vec{j}(\vec{r},t) = - \int_{\mathbb{V}_\text{A} + \mathbb{V}_\text{B}} d^3\vec{R}  \overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R}) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{R})),
\end{equation}
and for $\vec{r}$ located on the interface $\mathbb{S}_\text{AB}$:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:j_ss_at_interface}
\vec{j}(\vec{r}_\text{AB},t) = - \int_{\mathbb{S}_\text{AB}} d^2\vec{r'}_\text{AB} \overleftrightarrow{Z}_D(\vec{r}_\text{AB}, \vec{r'}_\text{AB}) \cdot \Delta T(\vec{r'}_\text{AB}).
\end{equation}

When the temperature jumps are uniformly $\Delta T$ at the surface $\mathbb{S}_\text{AB}$,  Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_at_interface} reduces to the Kapitza model with 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Z_to_Kapitza_homogenous}
\overleftrightarrow{G}_\text{K} (\vec{r}_\text{AB}) =  \int_{\mathbb{S}_\text{AB}} d^2\vec{r'}_\text{AB} \overleftrightarrow{Z}_D(\vec{r}_\text{AB}, \vec{r'}_\text{AB})   
\end{equation}
where $S_\text{AB}$ represents the surface area of the interface $\mathbb{S}_\text{AB}$.

\section{Unified Theory of Heat Conduction in Nonuniform Media}
\label{sec:general_theory}
\subsection{General Transport Equation}
\label{sec:general_transport_equation}
As detailed in Appendix~\ref{app:kernel}, statistical analysis of inhomogeneous phonon gases reveals that temporal memory and spatial nonlocality in the macroscopic heat flux, $\vec{j}(\vec{r}, t)$, can be rigorously described by a generalized constitutive law:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:J_expansion_r}
\begin{split}
\vec{j}(\vec{r},t)  = -& \sum_{n_1=0}^{\infty} \sum_{n_2=0}^{\infty} \sum_{n_3=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(n_1)! (n_2)! (n_3)!} \int_{0}^{\infty} dt' \overleftrightarrow{Z}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r}, t'; n_1, n_2, n_3) \\
&\cdot  \frac{\partial^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}} {\partial^{n_1} x \partial^{n_2} y \partial^{n_3} z} \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r},t-t').
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Here $\overleftrightarrow{Z}^{(n)}(\vec{r}, t'; n_1, n_2, n_3)$ are single-time convolution kernels encapsulating higher-order memory and nonlocal effects. Derivation details are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:kernel}. 

We propose that Eq.~\eqref{eq:J_expansion_r} holds for arbitrarily nonuniform media. Furthermore, it can be reformulated in terms of a compact spatiotemporal kernel function, $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$, defined over all point pairs $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{R}$ within a domain $\mathbb{V}$ of a heterogeneous material. This kernel governs the full space- and time-resolved response of the local heat flux to surrounding thermal gradients, systematically accounting for spatial inhomogeneity, temporal memory, and nonlocal interactions within a unified theoretical framework. The resulting transport equation takes the form:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:j_convolution}
\vec{j}(\vec{r},t) = - \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} \int_{0}^{\infty} dt'\, \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R},t') \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{R}, t - t'), 
\end{equation}
where the spatiotemporal heat conduction kernel function, $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$, replaces the conventional thermal conductivity, serves as the fundamental transport descriptor for heat conduction in nonuniform media, and the kernels $\overleftrightarrow{Z}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r}, t'; n_1, n_2, n_3)$ in Eq. \eqref{eq:J_expansion_r} are spatial moments of $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:spatial_moment_of_Z} 
\overleftrightarrow{Z}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r},t;n_1,n_2,n_3) = - \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r},\vec{R},t) {(\delta x)}^{n_1} {(\delta y)}^{n_2} {(\delta z)}^{n_3},   
\end{equation}
where $\delta x = X - x$, $\delta y = Y - y$, and $\delta z = Z - z$ denote the components of $\vec{R} - \vec{r}$.

Equation~\eqref{eq:j_convolution} generalizes earlier formulations, such as Eq.~(34) in Ref.~\cite{hua2020space} by Hua and Lindsay, which apply only to infinite, homogeneous systems. Their derivation assumes translational invariance and utilizes Fourier transforms to express the kernel as a function of the relative displacement $\vec{R} - \vec{r}$. However, this assumption no longer holds in spatially inhomogeneous media, where phonon spectra and scattering rates vary with position. In contrast, our formulation introduces a spatiotemporal kernel $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$ that depends explicitly on both spatial coordinates, allowing for a rigorous description of heat conduction in finite systems, across material interfaces, and within anisotropic domains. As such, Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_convolution} elevates the kernel function to a fundamental role in modeling thermal transport in heterogeneous and temporally evolving media.

Mathematically, the spatiotemporal kernel functions can be transformed into the frequency domain via a Fourier transformation in time, $t$, yielding the general heat transport equation in the $\omega$-domain:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Fourier_law_in_omega}
\vec{\tilde{j}}(\vec{r}, \omega)  = -  \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{\tilde{Z}}} (\vec{r}, \vec{R}, \omega) \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r\tilde{T}(\vec{R}, \omega), 
\end{equation}
where 
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:FT}
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:FT_j}
\vec{\tilde{j}}(\vec{r}, \omega) =  \int_{0}^{\infty} dt\, \vec{j}(\vec{r}, t) e^{i\omega t} \\
\label{eq:FT_gradientT}
\vec{\nabla}_r\tilde{T}(\vec{r}, \omega) = \int_{0}^{\infty} dt\, \vec{\nabla}_r\tilde{T}(\vec{r}, t) e^{i \omega t} \\
\label{eq:FT_Z}
\overleftrightarrow{\tilde{\mathbb{Z}}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, \omega) =  \int_{0}^{\infty} dt\, \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R},t) e^{i \omega t}.
\end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}

Unlike optical or electronic transport, where external driving fields are often directly frequency-controlled, thermal transport is typically governed by time-dependent temperature evolution. As a result, the time-domain formulation of heat conduction remains more physically intuitive and closely aligned with experimental observables. In prior work~\cite{crawford2024theory}, we demonstrated that the temporal conduction kernel $\overleftrightarrow{Z}(t)$ can often be approximated by a finite sum of exponential modes, each corresponding to a distinct phonon dissipation channel characterized by its relaxation rate. This structure facilitates both analytical treatment and numerical fitting of memory effects in transient heat flow.

The spatial heat conduction kernel at the diffusive limit, $\overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R})$, emerges as the steady-state limit of the full spatiotemporal kernel function, $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$, and can be formally obtained by time integration under steady-state conditions:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Z_to_K}
\overleftrightarrow{Z}_{D}(\vec{r},\vec{R}) = \int_{0}^{\infty} dt\, \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R},t).
\end{equation}


Similarly, the $\vec{r}$-resolved local conduction kernel, $\overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r}, t)$, can be derived from the spatiotemporal conduction kernel $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$ under the assumption that the spatial decay length of $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}$ is much smaller than the characteristic length scale over which the temperature gradient $\vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{r}, t)$ varies:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Z_to_z}
\overleftrightarrow{Z}(\vec{r},t) = \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} ~ \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R},t).
\end{equation}

Classical Fourier’s law emerges in the local and diffusive limit, wherein the conventional Fourier thermal conductivity tensor $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}(\vec{r})$ is recovered as the zeroth-order, steady-state limit of the spatiotemporal kernel function:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Z_to_kappa}
\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}(\vec{r}) = \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} \int_{0}^{\infty} dt\, \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R},t).
\end{equation}

Beyond this local limit, generalized thermal conductivity tensors, which are defined in Eq. \eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion} to characterize spatially nonlocal effects at the diffusive regime are given as:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Z_to_general_kappa}
\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r};n_1,n_2,n_3) = \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} \int_{0}^{\infty} dt\, \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R},t)\, (\delta x)^{n_1} (\delta y)^{n_2} (\delta z)^{n_3}.
\end{equation}


\subsection{Generalized Green-Kubo Formalism}
The classical Green–Kubo relation expresses bulk thermal conductivity as the time integral of the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the spatially averaged heat flux. In our framework, this concept is rigorously generalized to heterogeneous media by identifying the space- and time-resolved conduction kernel $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$ as the fundamental transport descriptor. The bulk Green–Kubo formula takes the form:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:green-kubo}
\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}_\text{bulk} = \frac{V}{k_B T_0^2} \int_{0}^{\infty} dt\, \langle \vec{j}_\text{bulk}(0) \otimes \vec{j}_\text{bulk}(t) \rangle_\text{eq},
\end{equation}
where $\vec{j}\text{bulk}(t)$ is the spatially averaged heat flux:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:average_j}
\vec{j}_\text{bulk}(t) = \frac{1}{V} \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{r}\, \vec{j}(\vec{r}, t).
\end{equation}
This leads to a double integral over spatially resolved heat flux correlations:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:j_coorelation}
\langle \vec{j}_\text{bulk}(t) \otimes \vec{j}_\text{bulk}(0) \rangle_\text{eq} = \frac{1}{V^2} \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{r} \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R}\, \langle \vec{j}(\vec{r}, 0) \otimes \vec{j}(\vec{R}, t) \rangle_\text{eq}.
\end{equation}
Comparison between Eq.~\eqref{eq:Z_to_kappa} and Eqs.~\eqref{eq:green-kubo}–\eqref{eq:j_coorelation} suggests that the space- and time-resolved heat conduction kernel function, $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$, which plays a central role in quantifying transient and nonlocal heat conduction in heterogeneous media, can be evaluated via numerical calculation of the space-resolved heat flux ACF:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:green-kubo_Z}
\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t) = \frac{1}{k_B T_0^2} \langle \vec{j}(\vec{r}, 0) \otimes \vec{j}(\vec{R}, t) \rangle_\text{eq}, 
\end{equation}
where $\vec{r}$-dependence encodes the inhomogeneity in the nonuniform media as this kernel becomes translationally invariant for $\vec{r}$ in the homogeneous limit. More generally, Eq.~\eqref{eq:green-kubo_Z} provides a first-principles pathway to extract the kernel from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations via evaluation of equilibrium heat flux correlations.

In summary, this unified theory systematically generalizes Zwanzig’s nonequilibrium statistical framework, rigorously incorporating temporal memory and spatial nonlocal effects into heat conduction. Starting from the homogeneous, local equilibrium limit, we progressively introduced hierarchical expansions to capture the emergence of memory and nonlocality, culminating in a full extension to spatially heterogeneous systems with both smooth and abrupt variations in material properties. This comprehensive framework offers a microscopically grounded yet computationally tractable methodology for modeling non-Fourier heat conduction across diverse material systems. The theory is encapsulated by the following set of three equations:
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:final_theory}
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:final_theory_conservation}
\rho C ~ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} T(\vec{r},t) + \vec{\nabla}_{r} \cdot  \vec{j} (\vec{r}, t)=0, \\
\label{eq:final_theory_j}
\vec{j}(\vec{r},t) = - \int_{\mathbb{V}} d^3\vec{R} \int_{0}^{\infty} dt'\, \overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R},t') \cdot \vec{\nabla}_r T(\vec{R}, t - t'),\\
\label{eq:final_theory_Z_end}
\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t) = \frac{1}{k_B T_0^2} \langle \vec{j}(\vec{R}, t) \otimes \vec{j}(\vec{r}, 0) \rangle_\text{eq}.
\end{eqnarray}
\end{subequations}

Beyond its theoretical role in transport equation, the kernel function also provides a direct link between nonequilibrium statistical theory and atomistic simulation. Traditional Green–Kubo methods use MD to estimate an effective thermal conductivity by time-averaging the autocorrelation of the total heat flux. While effective in the diffusive regime, this scalar reduction discards the spatial and temporal structure critical to understanding nanoscale and ultrafast transport. In contrast, the kernel formalism developed here enables extraction of the full space- and time-resolved conduction kernel, $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$, from MD simulations via spatially resolved equilibrium flux–flux correlations. This kernel captures how local heat flux responds to both delayed and distributed temperature gradients, offering a rigorous foundation for quantifying memory and nonlocality.

Rather than reducing simulation output to a single number, our framework transforms MD into a source of rich, position- and time-dependent transport information. This enables first-principles benchmarking of complex systems such as interfaces, nanostructures, and nonuniform media, where classical conductivity models fail. In this sense, the theory provides not only a unifying conceptual foundation, but also a practical platform for simulation–theory integration in the study of next-generation heat transport phenomena.


\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
We have presented a unified statistical theory of heat conduction that rigorously accounts for temporal memory and spatial nonlocality. By integrating the Zwanzig projection operator formalism with the phonon Boltzmann transport equation, we demonstrate that these non-Fourier effects originate from the statistical influence of \textit{irrelevant} microscopic degrees of freedom on the \textit{relevant} thermodynamic variable, the local temperature field, $T(\vec{r},t)$. These irrelevant variables can be categorized into two distinct classes: (i) flux-mode variables, which contribute directly to the macroscopic heat flux $\vec{j}(\vec{r},t)$, and (ii) nonlocal-mode variables, which describe higher-order deviations from local thermal equilibrium. Each mode is characterized by a finite relaxation rate, which sets the intrinsic memory timescale.

The macroscopic heat flux includes both a local, gradient-driven term and a nonlocal contribution that reflects spatial and temporal correlations among the underlying modes. This structure leads to a hierarchical, temporally nonlocal expansion, which we reformulate as a compact spatiotemporal kernel, $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$. This kernel provides a general, microscopically grounded transport descriptor for complex and heterogeneous media, extending the classical framework of heat conduction.

% The macroscopic heat flux comprises a local term, proportional to the temperature gradient, and a nonlocal term, arising from its coupling to gradients of the nonlocal-mode variables. All \textit{irrelevant} flux modes are mutually coupled through microscopic interaction parameters. This coupling leads to a hierarchical, temporally nonlocal relationship that produces a series expansion for the heat flux in terms of spatial gradients and their associated time-convolution integrals.

% We reformulate this infinite series into a compact spatiotemporal heat conduction kernel, $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$, which serves as the fundamental transport descriptor for general media. This kernel-based formalism naturally incorporates both smoothly varying and sharply discontinuous material heterogeneity, extending the classical framework of heat conduction. It establishes a new foundation for interpreting experimentally measured local temperature fields in terms of the underlying kernel function, rather than relying on conventional transport coefficients such as thermal conductivity or interfacial thermal conductance.

Our framework also enables new computational strategies for modeling heat conduction kernels in complex materials at the atomistic scale. Using first-principles or atomistic calculations of phonon spectra and scattering matrices as microscopic inputs, one can compute a finite set of spatial moments of the kernel function, such as $\overleftrightarrow{Z}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r}, t; n_1, n_2, n_3)$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:J_expansion_r} or $\overleftrightarrow{\kappa}^{(n_1+n_2+n_3)}(\vec{r}; n_1, n_2, n_3)$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:j_ss_expansion}, to approximately reconstruct the full spatiotemporal kernel $\overleftrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}(\vec{r}, \vec{R}, t)$ or its time-independent counterpart $\overleftrightarrow{Z}_D(\vec{r}, \vec{R})$. Alternatively, the kernel can be extracted directly from time-correlation functions of the space-resolved local heat flux density, $\vec{j}(\vec{r},t)$, obtained via molecular dynamics simulations or Fokker-Planck equation. Although evaluating the full kernel through time-correlation approaches is computationally intensive, recent advances in machine-learned interatomic potentials \cite{bartok2018machine} provide a promising path toward predictive modeling of heat transport in nanostructured and compositionally complex materials.

Finally, the kernel formalism is general and can be applied to other irreversible transport processes governed by Onsager reciprocity~\cite{onsager1931reciprocal,onsager1931_PhysRev.38.2265}. By generalizing classical transport coefficients to spatiotemporal kernel functions, our theory offers a unified platform for analyzing coupled transport phenomena in nonequilibrium systems.

% Finally, the spatiotemporal kernel formalism introduced here is not restricted to heat conduction. It can be naturally extended to other irreversible transport processes governed by the Onsager reciprocal relations \cite{onsager1931reciprocal,onsager1931_PhysRev.38.2265}. In this broader context, the conventional linear transport coefficients of classical irreversible thermodynamics are generalized to spatiotemporal kernel functions that describe the system’s full space- and time-dependent response. These kernels, defined via space- and time-resolved cross-correlation functions between distinct thermodynamic fluxes, recover the standard Onsager transport coefficients in the appropriate long-time and spatially averaged limits. As such, they offer a unified framework for analyzing coupled transport phenomena in nonequilibrium systems.
